_note: Narration script for the paramedic crush syndrome module (CPG-135-P v1.0, with ICP scope from CPG-136-ICP v1.1 and CPG-179-ICP). Lee voice on eleven_v4 (19 Oct 2026; an eleven_v3 take did not sound like Lee, so the owner asked for v4). Two takes joined (see overrides.json), short conversational sentences. The prompt sent to ElevenLabs starts with the [calmly] tag and spells IV, EOC, ICP, ECG, QRS, SAAS and RDR as letters, and mL/kg as "mils per kilo"; captions use the text here.

lines.head: What happens
sentences: A crush can come from a vehicle, falling debris, or machinery.
Or from someone who can't move, lying on part of their own body.
When it's released, the muscle reperfuses.
That's crush syndrome, or traumatic rhabdomyolysis.
Hypotension, acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

lines.head: Who to worry about
sentences: Not every crush leads to crush syndrome.
Anticipate it when the crush has lasted more than 60 minutes.
Over 18% of the body or more.

lines.head: Before release
sentences: Call the EOC Clinician for advice from the SAAS Medical Practitioner.
Two large bore IVs, if you can.
And start the saline before the crush comes off.
10 mL/kg aliquots, to a max of 250 mL.

lines.head: After release
sentences: Prioritise early transport, and keep scene time short.
10 mL/kg aliquots, max 250 mL, up to 20 mL/kg.
For children, aim for the low end of normal systolic for age, using the RDR.
Increasing jugular vein distension, or pulmonary congestion?

lines.head: The ECG
sentences: Consult the EOC Clinician about nebulised salbutamol.
It's a temporary fix, but it can help.

lines.head: When the ICP arrives
sentences: Your ICP works to their own guideline.
They can use the IO route.
And they treat hyperkalaemia under the hyperkalaemia guideline.
Calcium gluconate to protect the heart.

lines.head: Summary
sentences: Then watch the heart, and go.
